title: Your AI chat isn't a diary

beats: She used an AI chatbot like a diary. Then deputies showed up at her door.
Here's what's reported. September twenty-sixth, a Florida woman allegedly wrote she'd "shoot up" a sheriff's office. The next day, a message allegedly mentioned a new gun.
Anthropic says it monitors chats for threatening content. Serious flags can reach a human reviewer. Here, the team reported it to police.
September thirtieth: a felony charge for a written mass-shooting threat. Arraignment is November second. An allegation, not a conviction.
First time? No. Reports say at least two other chats reached police since August. San Antonio, a man arrested. San Francisco, no charges.
Not just one company. OpenAI has said chats about harming others can go to human reviewers, and imminent threats may go to police.
Anthropic's privacy policy, effective September tenth, allows disclosure when it believes that's reasonably necessary to prevent serious harm.
Its transparency report shows zero emergency requests from police in late twenty twenty-five. But it doesn't count reports the company makes on its own.
The sheriff says what you share with AI is "never truly anonymous." What we don't know: how often chats get flagged.
So, a chatbot isn't a diary. Safer, or watched? Tell me below. Follow for the next AI story.
